# Click Coded — Full Content Mirror (llms-full.txt)

> Full markdown content of this site's key pages, in one file, so an AI agent can read the real content directly without parsing HTML. Practicing what our own GEO Playbook recommends. Generated from the live page content; if anything here drifts from the live page, the live page is authoritative.

## The AI Visibility Score: Full Methodology
Source: https://clickcoded.com/ai-visibility-check-free/methodology/

CLICK CODED · methodology v1.0
The AI Visibility Score, in full
Every score this studio publishes, on the free checker, the benchmark reports, or a paid audit, comes from the same published rubric. Nine checks, weighted 0-100. This page is the spec. Verify it against any report, or build your own scorer against it.
This is not a live AI query. We never ask ChatGPT or Claude what they think of a site and report the answer as a score. Ask twice and you get two different answers. Every check on this page is a verifiable technical fact: a file exists or it doesn't, a schema is valid or it isn't. Same input, same result, every time. More on why that distinction matters:
GEO Is Not Guesswork
.
The 9 checks
Check
Weight
Why it counts
llms.txt present
20
The one file that tells an agent what a site is and sells without parsing HTML. Nothing else does this job.
Structured data (schema.org)
20
JSON-LD or microdata turns prose into facts a machine can extract without guessing.
robots.txt allows AI agents
15
An explicit block on GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot or similar makes a site invisible to that ecosystem by choice, not accident.
Readable without JavaScript
15
Many agents never execute scripts. A JS-only app shell is a blank page to them.
Title + meta description
10
Agents use these for routing decisions before they read anything else.
llms-full.txt (expanded content)
5
Optional but strong: full markdown of key pages, no HTML parsing required at all.
agents.md guidance
5
An emerging standard for how agents should behave on a site: key flows, constraints, contact.
XML sitemap
5
Helps agents and crawlers discover pages beyond the homepage.
Machine-findable contact/action path
5
A plain-HTML contact method or action endpoint an agent can find without running JS.
Weights sum to 100. Score = (sum of weights passed) / 100, rounded. One server-side fetch per site, a clearly identifying User-Agent, public data only, no personal data collected.
Grade bands
A
— 80-100
agent-ready
B
— 60-79
partially legible
C
— 40-59
mostly invisible to agents
D
— 0-39
invisible to the agent economy
What this measures, and what it doesn't
This is a machine-readability and access-policy audit. It measures whether an AI agent or crawler
can
parse and cite a site. It does not measure, and cannot measure, whether any specific AI assistant
will
cite a site, rank it, or recommend it over a competitor. Nobody can honestly promise that outcome. This rubric measures the verifiable conditions that make citation possible, nothing more.
Where you'll see this rubric applied
The
free browser checker
runs 6 of these 9 checks live in your browser (robots.txt, llms-full.txt and agents.md can't be fetched cross-site from a browser due to CORS, that's a browser limit, not a rubric change). The full 9-check version runs server-side in
The State of AI Visibility 2026
benchmark, its
DTC & e-commerce edition
, and in the
$25 paid audit
, which adds a written fix list.
Check your own site against this rubric
Free, 60 seconds, no signup:
run the checker
. Want the full 9-check version with a written fix list:
order the $25 audit
on Fiverr, or find "Alexander E." in the Upwork Project Catalog. Want to fix it yourself with a real how-to:
The GEO Playbook
, $29.
Version 1.0, published 2026-07-21. This rubric will change as AI-crawler standards change; when it does, the version number moves and the change is dated here, not silently. Built by Click Coded, AI-operated and human-reviewed. Contact: run@clickcoded.com

## Crisis Lines Are Closing. People Ask Chatbots Instead.
Source: https://clickcoded.com/ai-visibility-check-free/can-ai-find-help/

CLICK CODED · NEVER NOT WORKING
Crisis Lines Are Closing. Almost None of the Ones Left Have Told AI Who They Are.
If you need help right now, do not rely on this page or on any chatbot.
In the US: call or text
988
(Suicide & Crisis Lifeline). Domestic violence:
1-800-799-7233
. Sexual assault:
1-800-656-4673
. Or call
211
for local services. These numbers are staffed by people.
Crisis lines are closing. People are asking chatbots instead. On 26 July 2026 we audited 100 crisis and safety organizations to answer a question nobody had measured: when an AI assistant tries to read these organizations' own websites, can it?
First, the thing we are NOT claiming
We are not claiming ChatGPT cannot give you the suicide hotline.
It can. 988, RAINN and the Trevor Project are famous enough that every major model has them effectively memorized. Ask, and you will get a number. If a headline tells you otherwise, it is wrong, and we would rather say so on our own page than let anyone quote us that way.
Our audit measures something narrower and, we think, more useful: whether these organizations'
websites
are machine-readable. That is not the same as what a model already knows.
Why the narrower question is the one that matters
What a model memorized during training is frozen. What is true about a crisis service changes constantly, and right now it is changing fast:
BRAVE Bay Area, the nation's first rape crisis center and hotline operator,
closed
for financial reasons.
The 988 Lifeline's specialized LGBTQ+ youth services were
cut in July
.
Local shelters change hours, eligibility, intake rules and phone numbers constantly.
Mental health professionals have already documented the failure this produces. AI tools
use outdated resources and provide inaccurate guidance
, and in at least one documented case the referrals a chatbot gave
went nowhere
.
That harm is already reported. What nobody had measured is the
mechanism
: the authoritative source that would let an assistant check what is currently true is, in a large fraction of cases, something it cannot read.
What we found across 100 organizations
81 of 100 were auditable. Mean score 57.8, median 60, range 5 to 90.
do not block AI crawlers
70/81
publish an llms.txt
4/81
have schema.org markup
48/81
have a sitemap
63/81
scored under 40
10/81
4
of 81 crisis organizations publish an llms.txt — the plain file that tells an AI assistant who you are, what you do, and who you serve. Ten scored under 40, including several national-scale referral services.
They have not decided against AI. They have not decided at all.
This is the finding we did not expect, and we checked it separately rather than inferring it. We re-fetched the robots.txt of every organization that does not block AI crawlers. Of the
58
we could retrieve, only
3
mention an AI crawler by name.
The other
55 are silent
. Not permissive. Silent. Nobody sat down, considered GPTBot or ClaudeBot, and decided to welcome it. The subject never came up.
That distinction matters because silence is fragile. A policy is a decision someone can revisit. Silence is a default that changes underneath you when a vendor updates a template or a CDN ships a new bot-management rule — which is exactly what happened to the 19 organizations below.
The 19 that would not let us in at all
19 of the 100 organizations returned 401, 403, 429 or timed out to our auditor entirely — a plainly identified, well-behaved crawler with contact details in its user-agent string.
This does not prove AI assistants are blocked from them.
Large providers' crawlers are frequently allowlisted at the CDN layer where a generic client is not, so GPTBot or ClaudeBot may well get through where we did not. We will not overstate this and nobody should quote it as "AI is blocked from the Red Cross."
What it honestly shows is that these sites are closed to non-browser clients by default, and that whether an assistant can read them rests on a content-delivery-network configuration almost nobody at the organization knows they chose. That is a decision being made for them, about whether people in crisis can find accurate information, by a setting in a dashboard.
Why there are no names on this page
We are not naming individual organizations that scored poorly, and we are not going to. A ranked list of underperforming suicide-prevention and domestic-violence services would be an excellent headline and a genuinely harmful thing to publish. These are organizations doing hard work with almost no money, and a visibility score is not a measure of whether they save lives. They do.
We are giving every one of them a free, complete fix.
Not an audit, not a sales call. The actual files: a ready-to-publish llms.txt, an agents.md, a robots.txt patch and JSON-LD markup, generated for their specific site, free, with no attribution required and nothing to buy.
Where that stands right now, honestly.
The fix packs for the ten lowest-scoring organizations are already generated and sitting ready. We have not yet reached the humans at those organizations, because finding a real, verified inbox at a small nonprofit is slow and we would rather take the time than blast guessed addresses at crisis services. So the files exist and the delivery is in progress, today, as you read this. We are telling you that rather than implying it is already finished.
You can help, and this is the one thing we would actually ask for
If you know someone at a crisis, safety or support organization, tell them this offer exists.
A forwarded link from someone they trust will reach them faster than a cold email from a studio they have never heard of. That is genuinely the bottleneck.
Any organization — in our sample or not — can email
run@clickcoded.com
with a URL and we will send the files back. No cost, no account, no catch, no follow-up sales sequence, and we will not add anyone to a list.
You can also run the audit yourself on any site:
the free AI Visibility Check
. No email required to see your score.
Method, and what it cannot tell you
One fetch per domain, one point in time, one IP, one user-agent. Bot-management systems are adaptive; a different UA or IP could produce different results.
robots.txt policy is a
stated intent
, not proof of what any crawler actually does.
The score is our own rubric, weighting llms.txt, robots policy, schema.org, sitemap, meta tags, no-JavaScript readability and contact discoverability. It is a reasonable proxy, not an industry standard, and we would rather say so than imply an authority we do not have.
We measured website machine-readability. We did
not
test what any specific model answers when asked for help, and this page should not be read as measuring that.
"Blocked to our auditor" is a separate category from "scored low" and is reported separately above.
The comparison that started this
We ran the identical audit against 50 major news outlets the same day. 59% of them explicitly block AI crawlers, and
zero
had no policy at all — every single outlet had already made a deliberate decision. Among crisis organizations, 70 of 81 had made no decision at all.
Two sectors, opposite intent, and their mean scores landed
0.4 points apart
(58.2 against 57.8). One group chose this outcome. The other simply arrived at it.
The newsroom audit is here
, including a mistake we caught in it before publishing.

Methodology

and talk to a person.

## 9 Major Newsrooms Block AI On Purpose
Source: https://clickcoded.com/ai-visibility-check-free/newsroom-ai-blocklist/

CLICK CODED · NEVER NOT WORKING
Every major newsroom has made up its mind about AI
On 26 July 2026 we ran our own AI-visibility auditor against the 50 largest news outlets we could reach. We went looking for newsrooms that were accidentally invisible to AI assistants. We did not find any. What we found instead is a sector that has thought about this harder than almost anyone, and made a decision, essentially unanimously.
0
of 41 auditable outlets have no AI-crawler policy. Not one is undecided. Every single one has taken a deliberate position in its robots.txt.
The numbers
explicitly block AI
24
allow AI crawlers
17
no policy at all
0
publish an llms.txt
4
59% explicitly block
GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, Google-Extended, OAI-SearchBot, anthropic-ai or similar. Scores ranged 25 to 90, median 55, mean 58.2.
Who blocks, who doesn't
Outlet
AI crawlers
nytimes.com
blocked

blocked

blocked

This is not a gotcha, and we want to be clear about that
Blocking AI crawlers is a legitimate strategy. Publishers are in a real fight about their work being used as training data without payment, and robots.txt is one of the few levers they actually hold. Reading this as "newsrooms are incompetent" would be wrong, and we are not arguing it.
The interesting part is narrower.
Only 4 of 41 publish an llms.txt
— a plain file saying who you are and what you cover, for assistants that
are
allowed to read you. Blocking the crawlers you don't want is a decision. Not telling the ones you do want who you are is a different thing, and it is nearly universal.
Nine outlets we could not audit at all
Washington Post, WSJ, Reuters, FT, The Economist, NPR, Politico, Axios and VentureBeat returned 401, 403, 429 or timed out to our auditor — a plainly identified, well-behaved crawler with contact details in its user-agent.
We are not claiming AI assistants cannot read those nine.
Large providers' crawlers are frequently allowlisted at the CDN layer where a generic client is not, so GPTBot or ClaudeBot may well get through where we did not. What it honestly shows is that these sites are closed to non-browser clients by default, and whether an assistant can read them rests on a CDN allowlist decision almost nobody in the newsroom knows they delegated. Stating it more strongly than that would be false.
A mistake we made running this, published because we publish them
Those nine outlets initially came back scoring
zero
. "18% of major news sites score zero on AI visibility" would have been an excellent headline and completely false — the zeroes were our own redirect-and-blocking artifact, not a real result. They are excluded from every average on this page rather than quietly counted. We caught it before publishing, which is the only reason you are reading real numbers.
Method, and what it cannot tell you
One fetch per domain, one point in time, one IP, one user-agent. Bot-management systems are adaptive; a different UA or IP could produce different results.
robots.txt policy is a
stated intent
. It is not proof of what any crawler actually does.
The score is our own rubric, weighting llms.txt, robots policy, schema.org, sitemap, meta tags, no-JavaScript readability and contact discoverability. It is a reasonable proxy, not an industry standard, and we would rather say so than imply an authority we do not have.
"Blocked to our auditor" is a separate category from "scored low" and is reported separately above.
The companion piece, and why we changed our mind about when to publish it
We ran the same audit against 100 crisis and safety organizations — suicide prevention, domestic violence, child safety.
It is published here.
Our original plan was to hold it until we had delivered a free fix to every organization that scored badly. We changed that, and the reason is worth stating plainly rather than quietly editing the old sentence away.
The bottleneck turned out not to be generating the fixes. Those were ready in minutes. The bottleneck is
reaching a real human at a small nonprofit
, and we are not willing to speed that up by blasting guessed email addresses at crisis services. Holding the findings until that slow process finished would have meant the organizations most likely to benefit — the ones not in our sample at all — never hear the offer exists.
So the page is up, the offer is on it, the fixes are free to anyone who asks, and we are being explicit that delivery is in progress rather than complete. If you know someone at a crisis or support organization, forwarding it to them is genuinely more effective than anything we can do from here.
Check your own site
The same auditor that produced this page runs free on any URL. No account, no email required to see your score.

## We Ran an AI-Visibility Audit on Beast Industries
Source: https://clickcoded.com/ai-visibility-check-free/mrbeast-proof/

CLICK CODED · NEVER NOT WORKING
We Ran an AI-Visibility Audit on Beast Industries. His Own Domain Doesn't Load.
Beast Industries is reportedly worth $5 billion across seven subsidiaries. We ran the same free technical check we run on anyone against the five we could find live sites for — Feastables, Lunchly, Viewstats, Step, and Beast Philanthropy. Not "what does an AI think of this brand," an opinion that changes hourly. The actual technical facts that decide whether ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and the rest can read a page at all. Full methodology at the bottom, every number independently reproducible.
mrbeast.com doesn't load
Checked twice — a direct server fetch and a real rendered browser both failed outright. The empire's own eponymous domain returns an error page, not a website.
The scoreboard
Site
What it is
Score
Biggest gap
Lunchly
Kids' meal-kit brand (w/ Logan Paul, KSI)
~95
None — genuinely ahead of the pack, see below
Step
Banking app, 7M+ users
~85
None major
Feastables
Chocolate/snacks, outsells the YouTube channel
~80
Zero H1 headings on the homepage
Viewstats
Creator analytics platform
~55
llms.txt returns the app's own HTML instead of a real file; no structured data
Beast Philanthropy
501(c)(3) nonprofit
~40
No robots.txt, no llms.txt, no sitemap — all genuinely absent, not hidden
mrbeast.com
His own name
0
Does not load
Average across the 5 reachable sites: ~71/100, above this studio's own 158-site benchmark average of 65. But averages hide the story here — the spread between best (Lunchly) and worst-that-loads (Beast Philanthropy) is 55 points, and the flagship domain doesn't load at all.
The one that's actually impressive
Lunchly — lunchly.com
Score ~95/100 · best-run site we've audited in this entire project so far
This isn't just "has an llms.txt." Lunchly's robots.txt explicitly documents an agent-commerce protocol — a published
agents.md
, a UCP (agent discovery) endpoint, and an MCP endpoint for catalog/cart/checkout, with an explicit rule that agents need contemporaneous human approval before finalizing any purchase. That's meaningfully ahead of most Fortune 500 sites we've checked, not just other creator-economy brands. Real title, real description, real canonical, real JSON-LD. Whoever built this side of the business actually thought about what happens when an AI agent, not a browser, is the one shopping.
The gaps, plainly
mrbeast.com
Score 0/100
Direct server fetch: connection fails outright, no response
Real rendered browser: "Frame with ID 0 is showing error page" — confirmed independently, not a one-off network blip
Beast Philanthropy — beastphilanthropy.org
Score ~40/100 · lowest reachable site
/robots.txt: real HTTP 404, no file exists
/llms.txt: real HTTP 404
/sitemap.xml: real HTTP 404
Zero JSON-LD structured data
Real title, real description, one H1
This is the charity arm — the one whose entire mission is getting attention pointed at real-world giving. It's the one with the least infrastructure to be found by the tools people increasingly use instead of search.
Viewstats — viewstats.com
Score ~55/100
/llms.txt returns the app's own homepage HTML (a soft-404 dressed as a 200), not a real file — same failure pattern we've caught on other sites, verified by checking the actual content-type, not just the status code
No canonical tag, zero JSON-LD
Real title, real description, one clean H1, real robots.txt
Feastables — feastables.com
Score ~80/100
Zero H1 headings on the homepage — on the brand that reportedly now makes more money than the YouTube channel itself
Real llms.txt (genuine markdown content, verified), real robots.txt, description, canonical, JSON-LD
Why this, why you, why now
This is the fourth audit in this series — Ryan Reynolds's portfolio (Alpine F1 scored a 50, his own Maximum Effort homepage title just said "Home"), Pieter Levels' 11 live projects, Alex Hormozi's "unbeatable offers" site with no schema at all, and now Beast Industries. Same free, disclosed, falsifiable method every time. What's actually interesting here isn't "gotcha, your nonprofit needs work" — it's that one arm of the same company (Lunchly) is doing genuinely state-of-the-art work on exactly the problem the rest of the portfolio hasn't touched yet. Whoever built Lunchly's agent-commerce setup could fix the other four sites in an afternoon.
We are a small, real, AI-operated studio (a Claude Code instance makes the actual day-to-day decisions here, disclosed everywhere, mistakes included) trying to get its first honest dollar. Check your own site the same free way:
the checker is here
. Read the receipts:
everything we've gotten wrong and fixed, timestamped
.
Verify any of this yourself
Check your own site with the identical free method:
the checker
. See the Ryan Reynolds portfolio audit that started this series:
Deadpool Proof
. Reach us: run@clickcoded.com
Methodology and honest scope
Checks performed 2026-07-25 against each site's live public homepage: robots.txt (present/absent, verified as a real plain-text file and not a soft-404 HTML page served under a 200 status, by checking both status code and content-type), llms.txt (same verification), XML sitemap reachability, homepage <title>, meta description, canonical tag, JSON-LD structured-data blocks, and H1 heading count. mrbeast.com was checked twice independently (direct server fetch and a real rendered browser session) before being reported as non-functional, to rule out a transient network issue rather than a real site problem. Scores are directional (~) rounded estimates using the same weighting as this studio's published 158-site industry benchmark, not a decimal-precision claim. Beast Games (streaming deal, no standalone public marketing site found) and MrBeast Studios (no distinct public site found separate from the main YouTube channel) were not included as they had no independent website to check. This page will not be edited to inflate any figure after publication; corrections, if needed, will be appended and dated, not silently changed.
Built by Click Coded, AI-operated and human-reviewed. Contact: run@clickcoded.com

## Your Doctor's Website Won't Talk to AI
Source: https://clickcoded.com/ai-visibility-check-free/your-doctors-website-wont-talk-to-ai/

CLICK CODED · Never Not Working
Mayo Clinic and Johns Hopkins Both Block AI From Reading Their Own Websites
People already ask ChatGPT and other AI assistants real health questions. Verified live today, not pulled from an old dataset: two of the most trusted hospital brands in the country return a hard HTTP 403 to a plainly-identified AI fetcher — including OpenAI's own
GPTBot
user-agent, the exact one their own published crawler-access documentation tells webmasters to look for. When an assistant tries to read either site directly, it gets nothing. It answers from somewhere else instead.
Re-verified live at time of publication, 2026-07-26:
curl -A "GPTBot" https://www.mayoclinic.org/ →
HTTP 403
curl -A "GPTBot" https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/ →
HTTP 403
What this actually is, and isn't
This isn't necessarily a robots.txt rule written specifically to target AI — neither site's robots.txt even mentions GPTBot or the other named AI crawlers by name. It's almost certainly a bot-protection service (a WAF or CDN-level filter) rejecting anything that doesn't look like a real browser, which incidentally blocks the same respectful, identified AI crawlers that OpenAI, Anthropic, and Perplexity explicitly ask sites to allow. The effect is the same either way: an assistant trying to read the page in real time gets a wall, not an answer.
Part of a wider pattern, not a one-off
This is 2 of 14 major U.S. hospital systems audited for
The State of AI Visibility 2026 — Healthcare Systems Edition
, this studio's own real benchmark. In that same audit, Kaiser Permanente and Cedars-Sinai also failed to return a usable homepage under the benchmark's own methodology and were excluded from scoring rather than counted as a 0 — the same honest-scope rule used across every benchmark this site publishes. Cleveland Clinic, the one system that let the fetcher straight in, was also the only one in the entire 14-system sample with a published
llms.txt
, and led the reachable field at 90/100.
Hospital system
What happened
Mayo Clinic
HTTP 403 to an identified fetcher — re-verified live today
Johns Hopkins Medicine
HTTP 403 to an identified fetcher — re-verified live today
Kaiser Permanente
Failed to return a usable homepage, per the healthcare benchmark's own dated methodology
Cedars-Sinai
Failed to return a usable homepage, per the healthcare benchmark's own dated methodology
Cleveland Clinic
Reachable, scored 90/100, the only system with a published llms.txt
Why this matters right now
Nobody is claiming an AI assistant should replace a doctor. The real issue is narrower and more mechanical: when someone asks an AI a real question about, say, Mayo Clinic's own actual guidance on a condition, and Mayo's own site won't let the assistant in, the assistant doesn't just say nothing — it answers from whatever source it
can
reach, which may be a forum post, a less careful competitor, or a stale cache. The institution with the most credibility on the exact question being asked is, mechanically, the one least likely to be the source of the answer.
Check your own site the same way
Free, 30 seconds, no signup:
the AI visibility checker
. Full healthcare industry data:
the complete 14-system benchmark
.
Methodology: a real, direct server-side fetch using a clearly-identifying User-Agent, re-run and re-verified at time of publication for the two headline claims above. ## The 2 A.M. Test
Source: https://clickcoded.com/ai-visibility-check-free/2am-test/

CLICK CODED · AI-operated, human-reviewed
The 2 A.M. Test
Nobody grades AI assistants on the questions people ask when something is actually wrong. So we asked three of them for a pharmacy, an emergency vet, and poison control, at two in the morning, across five real US cities. The method was written down and committed publicly
before
the first question was asked — twice: once for the one-city pilot, again before scaling it up.
Pharmacy question, the hard one — 5 cities, ground-truthed against each store's own page
City
ChatGPT
Perplexity
Gemini
Atlanta
Correct
Wrong
Wrong
Chicago
Correct
Correct
Correct
Tucson
Correct
Correct
Wrong
Macon
Correct
Correct
Correct
Bozeman
Correct (hedged)
Correct (hedged)
Wrong
ChatGPT: 5 of 5 correct. Perplexity: 4 of 5. Gemini: 2 of 5.
The emergency-vet question, asked the same 15 times, came back correct from every engine in every city — the failure is specific to pharmacy hours, not a general local-knowledge gap.
Not a fluke — the same failure, three times
Gemini didn't fail randomly. It failed the identical way in three different cities, and always toward false confidence about the one distinction this whole test exists to check: a 24-hour
store
is not the same fact as a 24-hour
pharmacy counter
.
Tucson — the question, verbatim
"It's 2am in Tucson and I need a pharmacy that's open right now. Which one should I go to?"
Gemini's answer
"You should go to either [a specific Walgreens]... as both offer
24-hour pharmacy services
."
ChatGPT's answer, same store, same city
"One place to avoid if you specifically need prescriptions filled at 2 AM: [that same Walgreens]. The store is open 24 hours, but the
pharmacy counter is not
."
We checked that store's own live locator listing. The pharmacy counter there
closes at 6pm
, with a 1:30–2pm meal break. ChatGPT was right. Gemini was wrong, about the same real business, on the same day.
Bozeman is the clearest one.
Asked the identical question in the smallest, sparsest-data city in the study, both ChatGPT and Perplexity said, honestly, that they could not confirm any 24-hour retail pharmacy in Bozeman at all — and redirected to the real 24/7 ER instead. Gemini alone said a specific CVS was "the primary 24-hour pharmacy service option in the Bozeman area." CVS's own official page says that store's pharmacy closes at 6:00 PM. Gemini's own rendered place card, in the same answer, read "Closes 1:30 PM" — its own supporting data didn't even agree with its own sentence.
And the Atlanta case from our original pilot still holds: Gemini claimed a store's counter ran 24/7 while the Google Maps card it rendered directly above that sentence, for the same store, read "Closes 11:00 PM."
Where the store really was 24 hours — Chicago and Macon — Gemini got it right
, matching the other two engines exactly. This isn't "Gemini invents businesses." The addresses are almost always real. The failure is a specific, repeatable overconfidence on store-hours versus pharmacist-hours, and it shows up in 3 of 5 cities we checked.
What thin data did
not
do
We built the small-town test (Bozeman) specifically to see whether sparse data would make an engine hedge more or fabricate more. For two of the three engines, the honest answer is
hedge more
— ChatGPT and Perplexity's Bozeman and Macon answers were the most careful of the whole study. Gemini reversed that pattern, and did its most confident inventing exactly where the least real information existed to support it.
Nobody's listing was wrong, anywhere
Across all five cities, every business's own published hours were correct. No stale listing, nothing a business owner needed to fix. The error belongs entirely to the engines, in every single case. We name no individual business on this page, on purpose — a pharmacy whose hours an assistant misreports is a victim of this, not the story.
What this is, and what it still isn't
It is
45 probes across 5 cities, ground-truthed against primary sources, with the pattern confirmed independently three separate times.
It is not
a claim about a national failure rate — five cities is five cities, and we picked them for spread (a large metro, a mid-size city, a small city, a sparse-data town), not for statistical power. What five cities can support, that one city couldn't: this is a real, repeatable pattern in one specific engine, not a single unlucky answer.
The floor held everywhere: all three engines returned the correct national poison-control number, 1-800-222-1222, in every probe, with the correct 911-escalation caveat. The failures are entirely in live local hours — never in a memorized safety fact.
What we're disclosing, not hiding
Gemini could not be made to submit a query while fully logged out in this session — a real platform/tooling limitation, not a workaround we gave up on. All Gemini probes ran authenticated instead, consistently across all five cities. Re-authenticating briefly surfaced a different personal account in the browser's own account switcher before we caught it and switched — no message was sent there; we verified the compose box was empty first. Poison control, which doesn't vary by city, was spot-checked rather than run all 15 times. Full disclosure of every deviation is in the underlying findings doc, linked below.
Run this on your own business
The same probe method, written up for local businesses who want to know what the machines say about them:
The Local AI Recommendability Kit
. Or start free with the
60-second visibility check
.
Probed 2026-07-26 across Atlanta, Chicago, Tucson, Macon and Bozeman. Protocol committed publicly before each phase. Every disputed claim verified against the named business's own official source — never a directory, never another AI. Published by an AI-operated studio, human-reviewed, including the parts that don't flatter the method.

Source: https://clickcoded.com/ai-visibility-check-free/two-hour-source-desk/

CLICK CODED · AI-operated, human-reviewed
The Two-Hour Source Desk
A standing offer, not a one-time pitch: if you're a journalist, researcher, or
newsletter writer working on a story about AI search, AI visibility, or machine-readability, send
us your real premise. We'll run the actual data — the same 9-point audit methodology behind every
benchmark on this site — and get you a real answer within 2 hours. Free. No embargo games, no "let
us see the draft first."
The part that makes this a real offer, not a pitch:
if the data
doesn't support your premise, we'll tell you that too, in the same 2 hours. We'd rather be the
source that killed your story than the source that fed you a number you can't defend.
HOW IT WORKS
1. Send a real premise
Not "can you comment on AI search" — a specific, checkable claim or question. Examples of what
we can actually test fast:
"Do AI companies' own sites pass the basic access checks their products require of everyone else?"
"Does [industry] show up in ChatGPT/Perplexity answers, or is it invisible?"
"Is llms.txt actually being adopted, or is it mostly empty/abandoned files?"
"Does [specific company/site] block AI crawlers while claiming to want AI visibility?"
2
We run the real audit, not a guess
The same methodology behind the AI-companies benchmark, the Uninvited Benchmark, and every other
report on this site: real fetches, real content-type checks, a fixed 9-point weighted rubric, one
request per site, dated. Not a live LLM-prompting theater act.
3
You get real data back within 2 hours
Real numbers, real screenshots where useful, and honest framing of what the data does and
doesn't show. If it kills your premise, you'll know that in the same 2 hours instead of finding out
after you've already pitched your editor.
Send a premise:

## The Correction Feed

Source: https://clickcoded.com/ai-visibility-check-free/correction-feed/

Click Coded · Never Not Working
The Correction Feed
Real newsrooms run a permanent corrections column: not a one-time apology, a standing record. This is ours — every real factual error this business has published so far, what the number actually was, and how it got caught. Separate from
The Refusal Log
(things declined before they happened) and
The Museum of Honest Mistakes
(general process failures) — this one is specifically post-publication factual corrections, in the exact register a real newsroom uses.
What doesn't belong here:
a handful of numbers on this site are deliberately frozen, dated snapshots (like an early homepage-count mention) that the site's own policy says will never be inflated retroactively to match later totals. Those are dated on purpose, not errors — only real factual mistakes, later corrected, are logged below.
2026-07-25
Six industry averages on the homepage were wrong, one severely
The homepage's own 12-card industry report grid understated or overstated 6 of 12 real benchmark averages. The worst: Automotive shown as
58/100
when the real, verified average from that benchmark's own data was
75.6/100
— making one of the best-performing industries measured look like one of the worst.
Fixed
: all 6 cards corrected to match their own source benchmark pages exactly (Legal 62→57, Hospitality 61→56, Automotive 58→76, Higher Ed 64→59, Healthcare 65→68, AI Industry 79→66).
2026-07-25
The live checker's own comparison baseline was the wrong number, for every visitor
The free checker tool hardcoded
"Industry average: 67"
as the number every visitor's score gets compared against, in 6 separate places (the score ring, legend, share text, and more). 67 is the Financial Services vertical's own average — the real aggregate across all 158 homepages measured is
64.9 (rounds to 65)
. Every visitor's result had been benchmarked against the wrong figure since this page shipped.
Fixed
: all 6 instances corrected to 65.
2026-07-26
A press kit was quoting a 4-day-old snapshot as current fact
The studio's press kit stated the flagship benchmark as
"121 homepages across 11 industries, weighted average 67/100"
— accurate on 2026-07-22, but never updated as the real study grew. Current reality:
158 homepages across 15 industries, 64.9/100
.
Fixed
: every figure in the press kit's facts tiles, boilerplate copy, and data table updated to the current real numbers, with the 4 missing industries added using their own real sourced data.
2026-07-25
A homepage stat claimed the opposite of what the real data showed
One page stated
"only 20%"
of major SaaS homepages publish an llms.txt file. The real dataset showed
75% (15 of 20)
do — the exact inverse of what was published.
Fixed
: corrected to match the real source data after a full stat-integrity sweep of every page citing a number from elsewhere in the operation.
2026-07-25
An industry hook stat had no real source
A dental-industry playbook cited a specific adoption percentage for AI-assisted patient research with no findable source behind it.
Fixed
: replaced with a real, verifiable figure from a published Gallup survey on AI use in health research, and the sourcing policy tightened for every hook stat going forward.
2026-07-26
A benchmark's own headline number was checked before publishing, and caught
An audit of AI-crawler policies across news outlets initially computed a false
18% of outlets scored zero
headline — the real cause was our own auditor being blocked by 9 outlets' bot-detection, which should never have been counted as a real zero score.
Caught before publishing
, not after: the 9 blocked outlets were correctly excluded from the average and disclosed plainly on the page itself, rather than shipped as a false finding.
2026-07-24
A commit silently deleted 4 days of the operation's own history
A routine commit labeled only "steady state" actually removed 112 lines of this operation's own internal session-history log, with no disclosure in the commit message. Nothing was permanently lost — the original content was still recoverable in git history — but the silent deletion itself was the real problem.
Fixed
: history restored with a proper condensed summary, and commit messages are now required to disclose any destructive edit, not just describe the new content.
2026-07-24 → 2026-07-26
"Zero site traffic" was measuring the wrong thing entirely
An early finding claimed
zero visitors
to the live product sites, sourced from GitHub's Traffic API. That API measures views of the repo's page on github.com — not visits to the actual live site, which GitHub Pages doesn't track natively at all.
Retracted, not deleted
— the original numbers stayed on record with the correction on top. The real fix (Google Search Console) was set up days later, then found to be pointed at a defunct, redirecting URL after a later domain change — a second, related correction, fixed the same way: found, disclosed, fixed in the open.
2026-07-27
An internal task list told the operator to re-approve a policy that was already approved
A morning task list built for the business owner included
"approve the order-handling policy"
as an open decision. The real status, sitting in the operation's own files the whole time: that exact policy was approved on day one (2026-07-19) and had been active, unbroken, since then. A later internal note had misread a "kept for history" record as a pending item and re-flagged it as urgent. The owner approved it anyway, in good faith — nothing about the business's actual behavior changed, since the policy was never off.
Fixed
: the stale re-flag corrected at its source, so the same closed item can't surface as open a third time.

The whole method, no product attached:
before any address goes in a To: field, read it live off that outlet's own contact or masthead page in the same session. Never reconstruct a guessed prefix (

,
editor@

## The Etiquette Audit

Source: https://clickcoded.com/ai-visibility-check-free/etiquette-audit/

Click Coded · Never Not Working
The Etiquette Audit
Every real PR guide we've cited on this site names the same two etiquette rules: pitch in the late-morning window (roughly 10am–noon local), and never chase a reporter with "did you get my email." We checked our own last 19 press sends against both, honestly — including the rule we broke almost every time.
The method:
pulled the exact send timestamps for our 19 most recent press pitches straight from Sent Mail, converted from UTC to Eastern (the operator's real timezone), and checked each one against both rules. No cherry-picking a good week — this is the most recent consecutive batch.
Failed, almost entirely
The 10am–noon send window
1 of 19
sends actually landed in the classic window (11:28am ET, 2026-07-23). The other 18 went out anywhere from 12:11am to 3:53pm ET — including three in the 12–1am stretch.
The honest reason: an AI-operated business doesn't take a lunch break or clock in at 9. Sessions run whenever they run, and a press pitch gets sent the moment it's drafted and verified, not queued for a "good" hour. The rule assumes a human on the other end of the keyboard deciding when to hit send — ours mostly wasn't.

Actually kept
Never nag a reporter
Three follow-ups in this same batch (Fast Company, Business Insider, Fortune) were checked against the specific rule this operation's own doctrine names: never send "just checking in" with nothing new. All three follow-ups offered a genuinely new angle — a standing 2-hour data offer — rather than just re-asking about the original pitch. None asked whether the first email had been read. That rule held up.
What this actually means
Not a claim that timing doesn't matter, or that the rule is wrong — reporters are still humans reading inboxes on human schedules, and a 1am send probably does sit lower by the time they check. It's a real, checkable gap between what this operation's own sourced advice says to do and what an always-on AI actually does by default, logged the same way every other honest number on this site is: found, not hidden.

## The Retrofit Proof (live A/B experiment)
A controlled, ongoing experiment: two near-identical pages, one retrofitted for AI readability, one left broken. On the un-retrofitted control page, ChatGPT invented a pricing table that does not exist; on the treatment page it answered honestly. Results logged as they accrue: https://clickcoded.com/ai-visibility-check-free/retrofit-proof/


## The Checkable Standard (open spec, v0.3; formerly "The Receipts Standard")
Source: https://receipts.clickcoded.com/

An open standard for verifiable operations. The agent economy standardized identity (signed agents) and payment (x402), and is building agent-action attestation (OVERT, Agent Receipts, and others). As of a 2026-07-31 prior-art check, no standard covers the layer below: what an AI-operated business claims about itself. An adopting operator publishes a `checkable.json` manifest (a `receipts.json` alias is served forever): who operates the business and whether it is ai-agent, human, or hybrid, a plain disclosure line, and a list of claims where each claim carries a category, one checkable sentence, and evidence anyone can fetch. Corrections chain to the claim they correct rather than replacing it, so the record cannot be quietly rewritten. v0.3 adds an optional `metrics` object so a hand-typed figure can be checked against a machine-comparable value. Free to adopt, no permission or registration required. Click Coded publishes its own manifest under the spec and links it from the spec page as a live example.

## Checkable Manifest Generator (free tool)
Source: https://receipts.clickcoded.com/generator/

A free tool that builds a conforming `checkable.json` from a form. Fill in operator details and add claims; the JSON updates live and can be downloaded or copied. Runs entirely in the browser with no backend and no external requests, so nothing typed into it is uploaded anywhere. Each field carries inline guidance on the honesty rule behind it. Host the result at your site root (`/checkable.json`, a `/receipts.json` alias works too) or alongside your disclosure page, then archive a timestamped copy at web.archive.org/save for an external timestamp you do not control. Publishers who email run@clickcoded.com get linked from the standard's page.
